name: Starch: Nature's Energy Reservoir
notation_note: The alpha-1,4-linked glucopyranose unit is shown in condensed form (ring core plus three hydroxyls) -- the same sugar and the same formula as cellulose, joined the other way round, which is the whole difference between food and firewood. Real starch is a mixture of linear amylose and branched amylopectin, whose alpha-1,6 branch points are not shown.

historical_images.alt: Aerial view of steep, terraced rice paddies wrapped around a hillside village of thatched and tin-roofed houses, the paddies flooded and reflecting the sky.
historical_images.caption: Rice terraces in the Philippine Cordilleras, a form of cultivation practiced in Asia for over two thousand years — starch farming as old engineering.
historical_images.author: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas

historical_images.alt: Nineteenth-century engraved portrait of an older balding man in profile, wearing a dark coat, waistcoat and cravat.
historical_images.caption: Anselme Payen, whose 1834 memoir with Persoz first separated starch itself from the husk and fiber surrounding it in the plant.
historical_images.author: Jean Baptiste Adolphe Lafosse

historical_images.alt: Micrograph of many rounded, translucent potato starch granules under polarized light, each showing a bright four-armed cross of interference colors against a pink background.
historical_images.caption: Potato starch granules under polarized light. The crosses mark the semicrystalline layering inside each granule — order built for storage, not for strength.
historical_images.author: Photon 400 750

historical_images.alt: An 1876 bird's-eye engraving of a large riverside starch factory complex, with tall smoking chimneys, rows of multi-storey brick mill buildings, a rail spur, and horse-drawn wagons on the street below.
historical_images.caption: The Kingsford starch works at Oswego, New York, in 1876 — by then already one of the largest starch factories in the world, built on the same wet-milling principle used today.
historical_images.author: Unknown author

historical_images.alt: A small heap of pale yellow, cylindrical, foam-like packing chips on a dark background, with two loose pieces set apart from the pile.
historical_images.caption: Loose-fill packaging chips made from thermoplastic starch — a modern, compostable answer to the same question Payen was quietly answering in 1834: what, exactly, is this stuff made of?
historical_images.author: Christian Gahle, nova-Institut GmbH

density.conditions: 20 °C, native granules; varies by botanical source (e.g. maize, potato, wheat).

refractive_index.conditions: Potato starch, 25 °C, 589 nm; two principal indices reported (birefringent granules).

water_absorption.conditions: equilibrium immersion in water, 23 °C; equilibrium moisture uptake at 50% RH/23 °C is much lower, 10.2-13.3%.

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Not industrially polymerized -- biosynthesized in plants and harvested via wet milling: grinding, washing, and sieving to separate starch granules from other plant material (corn, potato, wheat, rice, cassava, and other crops), followed by drying. Enzymatic liquefaction (amylase) and saccharification convert starch into dextrins, maltose, and glucose syrups for many industrial uses.

crystallinity_typical.conditions: Native starch granules; wheat starch reported narrower at 32-36%. Becomes essentially amorphous after processing/gelatinization.

structure_morphology.crystal_structure: Semi-crystalline granules with concentric layering of amylose and amylopectin.

mn.conditions: Regular dent corn (maize) starch, whole granule, size-exclusion chromatography. Varies greatly with source: waxy maize 1.48e5, high-amylose corn 4.8-5.4e4.

mw.conditions: Regular dent corn (maize) starch, whole granule, size-exclusion chromatography. Varies greatly with source: waxy maize 2.18e7, high-amylose corn 3.96-5.75e6.

pdi.conditions: Regular dent corn (maize) starch. Waxy maize and high-amylose corn grades reported much broader, PDI 82-147.

tg.conditions: Native starch shows two transitions, -55 °C and 27-43 °C, both moisture-dependent; a much higher extrapolated Tg (~223 °C) is reported for anhydrous corn starch.

tm.conditions: Decomposes rather than melting; undergoes gelatinization in warm water instead of a true melt transition.

decomposition_onset.conditions: Estimated onset, reported under the DSC 'melting temperature' row since starch decomposes rather than showing a true melt endotherm.

tensile_modulus.conditions: Native/unplasticized starch; a much lower elastic modulus (9-38.7 MPa) is reported elsewhere in the same source, likely a plasticized or hydrated grade.

yield_strength.conditions: Tensile stress at yield; wide range reflects different starch products/grades and moisture content.

hydrolysis_resistance.value: poor -- readily hydrolyzed by acid and enzymes
hydrolysis_resistance.conditions: The alpha-glucopyranose linkage is more susceptible to hydrolysis/enzyme attack than the beta linkage in cellulose.

environmental.degradation_pathway: Enzymatic/microbial hydrolysis of glycosidic linkages; readily biodegradable.
environmental.environmental_notes: Renewable, widely used as a biodegradable-plastics feedstock (e.g. PLA precursor).

carcinogenic_classification.value: not listed by ACGIH, NIOSH, NTP

toxicity_safety.safety_notes: TLV (ACGIH) 10 mg/m³; OSHA exposure limit 5 mg/m³ (respirable), 15 mg/m³ (total dust).
